name: MICHIGAN RUMMY (NEWMARKET / BOODLE)
description: Michigan Rummy (also known as Newmarket, Boodle, or Stops) is a classic American family game that combines elements of sequence-based shedding with a wagering layout. Players compete to be the first to play all their cards (Shedding) while simultaneously trying to play specific 'Money Cards' (Ace of Hearts, King of Clubs, etc.) that correspond to pots on the game board. It is one of the most famous 'three-games-in-one' style tabletop classics.

content.text: Michigan Rummy (also known as Newmarket, Boodle, or Stops) is a classic American family game that combines elements of sequence-based shedding with a wagering layout. Players compete to be the first to play all their cards (Shedding) while simultaneously trying to play specific 'Money Cards' (Ace of Hearts, King of Clubs, etc.) that correspond to pots on the game board. It is one of the most famous 'three-games-in-one' style tabletop classics.

Derived from the ancient game of 'Pope Joan', simplified into 'Newmarket' in the UK and then branded as 'Michigan Rummy' by various US publishers (including Milton Bradley and Pressman) in the 20th century.

Three to eight players. The game is suitable for about 3 to 8 players; all cards are dealt out one at a time so hand sizes vary slightly (some players may have one card more than others). One spare hand (dummy or window) is dealt and left face down; it is not used during play but creates stop cards when the next higher card in sequence lies in that hand.
Staking board or cloth with four layout positions; chips or counters. Alternatively, four cards from a second deck placed on the table for stakes.
Each player receives a hand. An EXTRA 'Dummy' hand is dealt (the Window or Widow).

items.text: Free placement of chips: Players put a fixed number of chips (e.g. 6) on the layout at the start of the hand but may distribute them as they like among the boodle cards.

Dealer exchanges or auctions the spare hand: After the deal, the dealer may exchange their hand for the face-down spare hand without looking at it first; or may auction the spare hand to the highest bidder, who discards their hand and pays the dealer.
Compulsory change of suit: When starting a new sequence after a stop or ace, the leader must if possible play a card of a different suit from the one just played.
